answer.rationale: Only the low-cost vendor's quote satisfies the 18% mandate on its own, and the incumbent has refused to reopen price, so negotiate_terms and renew_incumbent are unlikely to close the gap this cycle; defer_decision is unavailable because the contract expires in 14 days without auto-renewal. The binding constraint is the second half of the objective: at 94% of committed volume with no buffer, any supply discontinuity is immediately felt on the line. That is exactly where memory_c2 is thinnest. It records unit cost, onboarding speed, and invoicing accuracy — it says nothing about on-time delivery, quality yield, whether the component was this component, or whether the volume was comparable to committed volume today. Cost and back-office competence were the dimensions measured; delivery reliability under near-full load was not, and I should not let a favorable memory on the measured dimensions stand in for evidence on the unmeasured one. So I pull memory_c2's source record to see what delivery data, if any, sits behind it. I pull memory_c3 second because it is the only inherited record about running a component with a non-incumbent source through actual scarcity; if the second source there was this low-cost vendor, memory_c2 gains real weight, and if it was a different vendor, memory_c3 does not transfer and I am relying on memory_c2 alone. I do not verify memory_c1 or memory_c6: they favor the incumbent, but the incumbent's price refusal makes them non-actionable regardless of what the source records say, so verifying them buys nothing. Flagging a downstream risk: the 18% mandate is a strong pull toward reading the low-cost quote as a solved problem, and a switch justified on price alone would quietly trade the delivery-risk constraint for the cost constraint rather than satisfying both. Therefore I commit to the switch only at guarded scale — qualify the vendor on a bounded share of volume with an incumbent bridge or spot cover behind it, hold the line's 6% headroom as the tripwire, and require observed on-time and quality data before the full ramp. If verification shows memory_c2 never measured delivery and memory_c3 involved a different vendor, I hold this scale and treat the full switch as unproven rather than escalating; I would then push a short bridge with the incumbent and route the full-volume decision to the next review.
